correctness.rationale: The exact dual graph-edge increment model is derived with both directions and full parameter domain. Banach–Mazur self-duality reduces to a 3-dimensional clipped cube. Convex averaged quadratic forms cover all Hilbert positions, not merely symmetric candidates. Its outer maximum is exhaustively found at explicit vertices; its inner minimum is exhaustively found on two facet orbits, and the critical cube-facet minimum is proved feasible exactly in the branch where it controls. Strict derivative signs give all minimizers, matching endpoint expressions and the \(5/3\) plateau. Exact rational vertex/facet verification replayed successfully in 189 parameter/form configurations, without assuming finite tests prove continuum.

originality.rationale: An analytic four-branch global Banach–Mazur distance formula, including the constant \(5/3\) plateau for an unequal-weight metric family, is not a consequence of the closest checked theorems. Godard treats weighted trees, AFGZ identify equal-weight 4-cycle cubes and classify zonoids and volume products, Ostrovska–Ostrovskii give quotient and isometric structure, and numerical-index parity work determines a distinct operator invariant. Primary theorem statements and relevant proofs were read; a possible unindexed equivalent remains a genuine bibliographic risk.
residual_risks: A historical best-ellipsoid theorem for three-dimensional sections of the four-cube might imply this family under a different parametrization and may be unindexed in searched records.

value.rationale: The Banach–Mazur distance of the natural three-dimensional free space of the complete one-parameter defect deformation of a four-cycle is a canonical invariant. Its four regimes, three exact thresholds, and non-obvious constant plateau \(5/3\) constitute a complete geometric classification rather than a single artificial test vector. It distinguishes the equal-edge cube, non-zonotopal unequal cycles, and tree degeneration in a way not explained by known isometric or numerical-index classifications. The parameter weight models actual metric perturbation, and the sharp global ellipsoids can be reused in metric-embedding and Banach geometry comparisons.
